details:
I really think you guys should take another serious look at whether Easy Anti-Cheat is still the right solution for the platform.

When EAC was introduced, one of the main arguments was that modified clients would be blocked and malicious client abuse would be reduced.

But years later, custom clients still exist.

Private clients still exist.

Bypasses still exist.

People are still developing tools that interact with the game in ways the official client does not allow.

So at this point, what is EAC actually controlling?

The people who genuinely want to build malicious clients are also the people willing to spend weeks or months researching ways around whatever protection is put in front of them.

Meanwhile, regular users are the ones who are consistently blocked from harmless modifications, accessibility tools, QoL improvements, debugging utilities and other experimental features.

At the end of the day, this is software running on hardware controlled by the user.

Like no client-side anti-cheat can guarantee forever that an application cannot be inspected, modified, hooked or emulated.

The better security model is to assume the client is untrusted and make sure everything important is validated somewhere you actually control.

A custom client existing should not automatically be dangerous.

The dangerous part is what your servers allow that client to do.

Things like:

- invalid network events

- event or RPC spam

- broken ownership transitions

- impossible player states

- automated abuse

- malformed protocol data

- unauthorized instance actions

- asset-related abuse

- API abuse

should be handled as much as possible by your own protocol, backend and validation logic.

The model should be closer to:

untrusted client -> strict validation -> limited authority -> backend

not:

EAC -> client is trusted enough

because once someone gets around the first layer, that assumption becomes much weaker.

This is the biggest point for me.

Custom clients are still around.

People still advertise private builds.

Modified-client reports still happen.

There are still tools and abuse cases that clearly require functionality outside of the normal client.

So the original idea that EAC would solve the modified-client problem should be re-evaluated.

I'm not saying EAC does absolutely nothing.

I'm saying you guys should be able to answer some basic questions in 2026:

- What attacks is EAC actually stopping today?

- Which abuse cases specifically depend on EAC?

- How many of the original problems from 2022 are still prevented mainly by EAC?

- How much abuse currently comes from clients that already bypass it?

- Could more of this protection be moved into the backend or protocol?

- Is the cost of blocking all client modification still worth it?

It would be good to see an updated explanation instead of relying forever on the reasoning from 2022.

The client has now moved to Unity 6, which is a pretty major technical change.

I'm not claiming that Unity 6 magically makes EAC useless.

The point is that when you move to a newer engine/runtime and rebuild a large amount of client-side infrastructure around it, that is exactly the kind of moment where old security assumptions should be reviewed.

A lot has changed since EAC was originally introduced.

So this seems like a reasonable time for the dev team to ask:

If you were designing the current security model from scratch today, for the Unity 6 client, would you still choose exactly the same approach?

If yes, explain why.

If not, maybe it is time to start changing it.

The long-term goal should be that even a fully modified client cannot do anything particularly dangerous.

If someone sends something the normal client would never send, reject it.

If somebody tries to perform an action they should not be allowed to perform, reject it.

If a client starts spamming events at impossible rates, rate-limit it.

If ownership changes do not make sense, validate them.

If automation starts behaving in a way a real player realistically would not, detect it.

If an API action is being abused, block it at the API level.

Those protections still work even when the attacker completely controls their own client.

That is much stronger than relying mainly on stopping them from modifying the client in the first place.

I also think the team should separate these two concepts more clearly.

There is a massive difference between client made to crash other users and a modification adding an accessibility feature, so

There is a difference between malicious automation and UI customization.

There is a difference between stealing assets and exposing additional local performance information.

The security target should be abusive capabilities and unauthorized actions.

Not modification itself.

If unrestricted client mods are considered too risky, there is still a middle ground.

You could expose an official extension system with sandboxed plugins and explicit permissions.

For example, extensions could be allowed to work with:

- UI

- accessibility

- OSC

- local performance data

- tracking integrations

- creator tools

- hardware integrations

while being completely blocked from sensitive areas such as authentication data or unrestricted internal networking.

Extensions could be:

- sandboxed

- permission-based

- signed

- versioned

- revocable

- limited to documented APIs

That would give the dev team much more control than the old unrestricted modding ecosystem while still allowing useful experimentation.

It would also remove a lot of the incentive for normal users to look for unofficial clients just to get features missing from the official one.

Nobody is asking you guys to remove security.

The point is to review whether the current approach still makes sense.

It has been years.

The client changed.

The engine version changed.

The platform changed.

The threat model changed.

And custom clients are still here.

Security decisions should be based on how well they work now, not only on why they were introduced years ago.

The goal should not be: "make client modification impossible."

The goal should be: "even if someone modifies the client, they still cannot meaningfully abuse the platform or other users."

That is a much stronger security model.

I would genuinely like to see the team re-evaluate whether EAC in its current form is still the best way to get there.
title: Re-evaluate Easy Anti-Cheat and the current security model
